full_judgment:
2. Relevant facts are summarized as follows: Plaintiffs filed the aforesaid title suit for a declaration of title and confirmation of possession or in the alternative for recovery of khas possession of the suit land on the allegations that they as benamdar of the judgment-debtors auction purchased a jote which included 5.33 acres of tenanted land under Khatian No. 99 standing in the names of Panchy Sheikh, Kamaruddin Sheikh i.e. the father of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and Ramjan i.e. the father of the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 in Rent Execution Case No.1035 of 1930 arising out of Rent Suit No. 607 of 1930 on 20-1-1931 and took delivery of possession thereof on 2-5-1931 after having annulled the encumbrance namely, the said under-tenancy by service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Father of defendant Nos.1 and 2 late Kamaruddin Sheikh having admitted annulment of the said under-tenancy took fresh settlement of some of the said under tenancy by executing kabuliayat. But due to mistake 2.30 acres of land of the said under-tenancy was wrongly recorded in the names of the defendants during SA settlement and by taking advantage of such wrong recording the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from the said land on 21st Chaitra 1373 BS. Hence the plaintiffs were constrained to file the suit. 

 3. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement asserting that their under-tenancy was never annulled and they were all along in possession. The defendants denied that late Kamaruddin or Samajuddin ever executed any Kabuliyat admitting annulment of their under tenancy or taking over Khas possession of the same by the plaintiffs stating that if there was any Kabuliyat by Kamaruddin that must have been manufactured for the purpose of the case. The defendants further asserted that since there was no annulment of the under-tenancy in question the suit land was recorded in the name of the predecessors-in-interest of the defendants during the petty and revisional settlement that took place after the purported auction-sale. Subsequently the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants during the SA settlement. 

 4. Both the trial Court as well as the first appellate Court below decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs succeeded in proving the service of notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act annulling the under-tenancy in question and that they were in possession of the suit land holding that although the plaintiffs could not prove the service of notice of annulment of the under-tenancy in question in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act by producing any paper, but admission of late Kamaruddin i.e. the father of the defendants Nos.1 and 2 and Mominuddin i.e. the defendant No.6 (not an under-tenant) and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sufficiently proved service of notice. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred this Second Appeal. 

 5. Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below earred in law in holding that the plaintiffs as auction-purchasers annulled the under tenancy in question by serving notice on the under-tenants in terms of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, although they (plaintiffs) failed to prove the service of notice as required in law. Learned Advocate also submits that the courts below also erred in law in failing to appreciate that since the plaintiffs as benamdars of the judgment-debtors were debarred under section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act from auction purchasing the suit land no notice under section 167 of the Act was served by the Court which held the auction-sale. 

 7. The moot question requiring determination is whether the respondents succeeded in proving the annulment of the encumbrance, namely, the under-tenure of the appellants, by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The question whether notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was duly served in this case is a question of law. Hence the concurrent finding of the Courts below on this point is liable to be interfered with by this Court in case such finding is bad in law. 

 8. A sale in execution of a rent decree will ipso facto cancel an encumbrance. Until an encumbrance namely, the under-tenancy, as in this case, is annulled by notice as required under section 167 of the Bengali Tenancy Act the under-tenancy subsists vide AIR (1929) Cal. 392. If an auction-purchaser in a rent sale desires to exercise his power of annulment of any encumbrance he is required to strictly comply with the requirements of section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act as regards service of notice and such notice must be served within one year from the date of confirmation of sale or from the date of knowledge thereof whichever date is later. 

 10. Purchaser is under obligation to show that the notice under section 167 has been served in the manner provided under this section, namely, that he made an application to the Court or the revenue officer in writing requesting him to serve on the encumbrancer a notice declaring that the encumbrance is annulled. Notice of annulment is to be served in the manner provided for the service of summons under Order 5, rules 11 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure as required by the Rules framed by the Government under sections 189 and 190 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The case of Ananda Gopal vs Nafar Chandra reported in 18 CWN (PC) 259 is an authority on this point. The purchaser must prove service of notice by the production of the person who served it or by any other means recognized by law vide 7 CLJ 262. Even the entries in the order-sheet of the Court which caused the notice to be served on the application of the purchaser are not the prime evidence against the encumbrance that the notice was served. 

 11. In the instant case, respondents have admittedly failed to produce any paper in support of service of notice under section 167of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The finding of the Courts below, particularly the appellate Court below that service of such notice as well as possession of the suit land by the respondents have been proved by admission of the appellant Nos.1 and 2 and their father late Kamaruddin and also by admission of defendant No.6 Mominuddin is erratic and perverse being contrary to law and evidence. The decision reported in 37 DLR 126 is not applicable in the present case as the facts are distinguishable. The defendant No.6 is not an under-tenant but apparently a camp-follower of the respondents and accordingly, he deposed as PW 2 stating in his evidence that notice was served in his presence. Such admission by defendant No.6 cannot be a proof of service of notice as contemplated under Section 167. 

 12. Respondents are admittedly the benamdars of the judgment-debtors. Section 173 of the Bengal Tenancy Act debars the judgment-debtors as well as their benamdars from purchasing any defaulting tenure. A judgment debtor or his benamdar purchasing the defaulting tenure, even if the sale is allowed to stand, is not entitled to annul the encumbrance. The case of Fakir Chander Dutt and others vs Ram Kumar Chatterji reported in 8 CWN (PC) 721 is referred to in this connection. Since the service of notice under section 167 in this case has not been proved as proscribed by law the encumbrance in question still subsists. Accordingly, the finding of possession of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs by the Courts below is not sustainable in law. Therefore, the contention that the plaintiffs have acquired title by adverse possession is not acceptable.
